section.heading: Article Overview
description: Acne is one of the most common skin conditions in the world, affecting people of all ages and skin types. Yet, despite how widespread it is, most people don’t fully understand what causes it or why it tends to show up in certain areas like the back, jawline, or cheeks.
In this article, we break down the real science behind acne — What acne is, what are the symptoms of acne, what causes acne, how it forms, internal root causes, other triggers.

section.heading: What Is Acne?
description: Acne forms when the pores on your skin become clogged with a combination of excess oil (sebum), dead skin cells, and bacteria. This blockage leads to inflammation — causing the pore to swell, appear red, and sometimes develop into painful bumps or pus-filled lesions.

But acne isn’t just a surface-level issue. It’s often the result of deeper internal factors like hormones, stress, and gut health interacting with external influences such as skincare habits, pollution, and hygiene. Understanding both sides is key to managing it effectively.

section.heading: What are the symptoms of acne?
section.text: Acne isn’t just one kind of bump — it appears in different forms, each with its own severity and underlying cause. Here’s a breakdown of the most common types:

subSections.title: Whiteheads
points: Small, closed pores clogged with oil and dead skin cells. They appear as white or flesh-colored bumps and do not open at the surface.

subSections.title: Blackheads
points: Open pores filled with excess oil and dead skin. When exposed to air, the material oxidizes, giving the bump a dark or black appearance.

subSections.title: Papules
points: Red, inflamed bumps that don’t contain pus. They are usually tender and form when pore walls break down from inflammation

subSections.title: Pustules
points: Papules that develop a visible white or yellow center of pus, surrounded by red, inflamed skin. These are often what people refer to as “typical pimples.

subSections.title: Nodules
points: Large, painful lumps that form deep under the skin. They are firm to the touch, do not contain pus, and take longer to heal.

subSections.title: Cysts
points: Deep, soft, pus-filled lesions that can be painful and often leave behind scars. Cystic acne is typically the most severe form and may persist for weeks.

section.heading: The Science Behind Acne Formation
section.text: Acne begins deep within the skin — long before any visible breakout appears. Here’s a simplified breakdown of what’s happening beneath the surface:

subSections.title: Sebum production increases
points: Your sebaceous (oil) glands naturally produce sebum to keep skin moisturized. But when they produce too much, problems begin.

subSections.title: Dead skin cells build up
points: Normally, dead skin sheds on its own. But when it doesn’t, it mixes with excess sebum and clogs the pore.

subSections.title: Bacteria multiply
points: The blocked pore creates the perfect environment for Cutibacterium acnes (a common skin bacteria) to grow rapidly.

subSections.title: Inflammation sets in
points: As the body reacts to the bacterial buildup, the area becomes inflamed — leading to redness, swelling, and discomfort.

subSections.title: Visible acne forms
points: Depending on the depth and severity of the blockage and inflammation, this can result in whiteheads, papules, pustules, cysts, or nodules.
Though it may seem like a surface concern, acne is actually an inflammatory condition rooted in skin biology and immune response.

section.heading: Who gets acne?
section.description: Acne can affect anyone — it doesn’t discriminate by age or gender. While it’s most common during certain life stages, it can show up at any time due to different triggers

subSections.title: Teenagers
points: Hormonal changes during puberty often lead to increased oil production, making breakouts more likely.

subSections.title: Adults (especially women)
points: Hormonal fluctuations related to menstrual cycles, PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome), pregnancy, or chronic stress can trigger adult acne — especially around the jawline or chin.

subSections.title: Men
points: Men may be more prone to inflammatory acne or breakouts on the chest, shoulders, and back due to higher sebum production.

subSections.title: Infants
points: Newborns can experience baby acne in the first few weeks of life, typically due to residual maternal hormones. It usually clears up on its own.

section.heading: Where on the Body Can Acne Appear?
section.text: Acne isn’t limited to the face — it can develop anywhere on the body where there are oil glands and hair follicles. Some areas are more prone due to sweat, friction, or hormonal activity:
points: Face: The most common area — especially the forehead, nose, chin, and cheeks — due to high oil gland activity.
Back (often called “bacne”): Common in people who sweat more or wear tight clothing. Friction, heat, and oil buildup contribute to breakouts.
Chest and shoulders: Frequently seen in men, especially those with higher sebum production or those who work out regularly.
Jawline: Often linked to hormonal fluctuations or conditions like PCOS. Breakouts here are typically deeper and more persistent.
Neck, upper arms, and buttocks: These areas can also develop acne-like lesions, often triggered by friction, sweat, or keratin buildup in hair follicles.

section.heading: Internal Root Causes of Acne
section.text: While skincare and hygiene play a role, many cases of acne are driven by what’s happening inside the body. These internal factors can trigger excess oil production, inflammation, or changes in skin cell turnover:
points: Hormonal Imbalances: Shifts in hormones — especially androgens — can increase oil production and lead to clogged pores. This is common during puberty, menstrual cycles, pregnancy, or in conditions like PCOS.
Stress: Chronic stress triggers the release of cortisol and other hormones that can increase oil production and inflammation, worsening acne.
Diet and Blood Sugar Spikes: Diets high in processed carbs, sugar, and dairy may influence hormones like insulin and IGF-1, which can stimulate sebum production and inflammation.
Gut Health: Imbalances in the gut microbiome may contribute to systemic inflammation, which can show up on the skin as acne. Poor digestion or food sensitivities can also play a role.
Genetics: If your parents had acne, you're more likely to experience it too. Genetics can influence how much oil your skin produces, how it responds to bacteria, and how quickly skin cells shed.

section.heading: Everyday Triggers That Can Worsen Acne
section.text: Even when internal causes are addressed, everyday habits can quietly contribute to breakouts. These external triggers often go unnoticed but can play a significant role in keeping acne active:
points: Unwashed pillowcases and towels: Fabric that touches your face regularly can accumulate oil, bacteria, and product residue — transferring it back to your skin.
Pollution and environmental dust: Fine particles in the air can settle into pores, especially in urban areas, contributing to congestion and inflammation.
Heavy or comedogenic makeup: Thick, oil-based products can block pores — particularly if not fully removed at night.
Hair products: Oils, sprays, and gels can transfer to the forehead or jawline, triggering breakouts around the hairline or face.
Tight or sweaty clothing: Staying in workout gear too long can trap sweat and bacteria against the skin, especially on the back, chest, and shoulders.
Touching your face frequently: Your hands carry bacteria and dirt that can easily transfer to your skin — especially when resting your face on them.
Dirty phone screens and makeup brushes: These surfaces come in close contact with your skin and can harbor oil and bacteria if not cleaned regularly.
Skipping cleansing after workouts: Sweat left on the skin can mix with oil and clog pores — cleansing soon after is essential to prevent buildup.

section.heading: Final Thoughts
description: Acne is more than just a surface concern — it’s often your skin’s way of signaling internal imbalances or lifestyle stressors. Whether it’s driven by hormones, diet, poor cleansing habits, or underlying inflammation, understanding the root cause is key to managing it effectively.

While quick fixes may offer short-term relief, true skin clarity comes from a deeper understanding of what’s triggering your breakouts. If you're noticing consistent patterns — like acne along the jawline, back, or cheeks — it may be time to look beneath the surface and address the real cause, not just the visible symptoms.

description: At Clear Ritual, we believe acne deserves a more thoughtful approach — one that’s based on your unique skin type, acne pattern, and internal triggers. Our goal is to simplify acne care by helping you identify what’s really going on, so you can start a regimen that actually works.

section.heading: Article Overview
description: Acne is often seen as one single skin condition, but in reality, not all breakouts are the same. Treating every pimple the same way can lead to confusion, frustration, and results that don’t last. Two of the most common — and most misunderstood — forms are hormonal acne and bacterial acne. While they can look similar, they’re caused by very different internal and external factors, and each type responds to treatment in its own way.

In this article, we explore the difference between hormonal and bacterial acne, explain how each one shows up, what causes it, and why knowing the difference can completely change how you approach your skincare.

section.heading: What Is Hormonal Acne?
description: Hormonal acne is driven by changes in your hormone levels — especially androgens, like testosterone. These hormones signal the skin’s oil glands to produce more sebum. When there’s too much oil and not enough natural shedding of dead skin cells, pores get clogged. This sets off a chain reaction of inflammation and breakouts, often below the surface of the skin.

section.heading: Who Gets Hormonal Acne?
description: This type of acne isn’t limited to teenagers. It often affects adult women with menstrual cycles, PCOS, or other hormonal imbalances. Many people also experience hormonal acne during puberty, pregnancy, postpartum recovery, or menopause. Even men can develop hormonal acne — especially those with high testosterone levels or those using anabolic steroids.

section.heading: What Triggers Hormonal Acne?
description: The most common triggers include sudden spikes in androgen levels, shifts in estrogen and progesterone during menstrual cycles, or underlying conditions like PCOS. Stress is another major factor — it increases cortisol, which indirectly stimulates more oil production. Hormonal acne can also be affected by pregnancy, when your hormone levels fluctuate dramatically. Some women find their skin clears up during pregnancy, while others experience breakouts, especially in the first trimester.

section.heading: Are There Lifestyle Factors That Worsen It?
description: Yes, and many are easy to overlook. Diets high in sugar or dairy may influence insulin and androgen levels, which can increase oil production. Poor sleep or irregular sleep cycles may also disrupt hormonal balance. Daily stress, heavy makeup, skipping post-workout cleansing, and not tracking changes in your skin throughout your cycle can all contribute to more frequent breakouts.

section.heading: What Does Hormonal Acne Look Like?
description: Hormonal acne usually appears as deep, painful pimples — often cystic and located under the skin. These breakouts tend to show up around the jawline, chin, and lower cheeks, and they often return in the same areas each month, especially before menstruation. Hormonal acne also tends to resist standard over-the-counter products and may be accompanied by other symptoms, such as irregular periods or hair thinning.

section.heading: When Should You Start Treating Hormonal Acne?
description: The sooner you address hormonal acne, the better. Early treatment helps reduce inflammation, prevent scarring, and avoid long-term flare-ups. If your acne follows a monthly pattern, is painful or deep, doesn’t respond to drugstore products, or comes with other signs of hormonal imbalance, it’s time to consider a targeted plan that includes both internal and topical support.

section.heading: What Is Bacterial Acne?
description: Bacterial acne is caused by the overgrowth of Cutibacterium acnes, a bacteria that naturally lives on the skin. This bacteria thrives in clogged pores, where it feeds on trapped oil. As it multiplies, it triggers inflammation and pus formation, which leads to visible breakouts. Unlike hormonal acne, bacterial acne is more often linked to external triggers like sweat, friction, heavy skincare products, or unclean surfaces.

section.heading: How Do Hormonal and Bacterial Acne Differ?
description: While both types involve clogged pores and inflammation, their causes — and how they show up on your skin — are very different.

Hormonal acne usually appears on the lower half of the face: the chin, jawline, cheeks, and sometimes the neck. It tends to be deep, tender, and recurring, often flaring just before a period or during major hormonal shifts like puberty or pregnancy. It doesn’t always respond to surface-level treatments and typically requires a plan that addresses internal balance — whether that’s through lifestyle changes, prescription support, or both.

Bacterial acne, on the other hand, shows up more frequently on the forehead, nose, upper back, and shoulders. It may present as clusters of whiteheads, pustules, or red bumps that respond better to antibacterial and exfoliating products. It’s often made worse by excess sweating, occlusive makeup or skincare, dirty pillowcases, unwashed makeup brushes, or poor post-workout hygiene.

Understanding what type of acne you're dealing with is crucial. Hormonal acne requires addressing the internal cause — like hormones and inflammation — while bacterial acne is more responsive to cleansing, exfoliation, and proper barrier care.

description: At Clear Ritual, we believe acne care should go deeper than surface-level spot treatments. Whether your breakouts are hormonal, bacterial, or a mix of both, real results begin with understanding what’s causing your acne — not just what it looks like.

Our science-backed routines are designed around your unique skin type, acne pattern, and internal triggers. Take our free skin test to uncover the true cause of your acne and get a personalized plan designed to work with your skin — not against it.

A Note from the Clear Ritual Team

section.heading: Article Overview
description: Not all acne is the same — and if your breakouts keep recurring in the same spots, especially around your jawline or chin, there’s a good chance your acne is hormonal. Unlike bacterial or comedonal acne, hormonal acne is rooted in internal imbalances, meaning treating it effectively requires a different approach.
In this article, we’ll break down the key signs, symptoms, and patterns that suggest your acne might be hormonal — and what you can do about it.

section.heading: What Is Hormonal Acne?
section.text: Hormonal acne is caused by fluctuations in hormones, particularly androgens like testosterone. These hormones increase the activity of sebaceous (oil) glands, leading to excess sebum, clogged pores, and inflammatory breakouts. It’s especially common during:
points: Puberty
Menstrual cycles
Pregnancy or postpartum
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
Perimenopause or menopause
section.paragraph: It can also appear in individuals under high stress or with insulin resistance and gut dysbiosis — both of which impact hormone pathways.

section.heading: How to Tell If Your Acne Is Hormonal

section.title: 1. Location of Breakouts
section.text: Hormonal acne has a distinct pattern. It most commonly appears on the lower face, including the:
points: Chin
Jawline
Neck
Sometimes the cheeks
section.paragraph: This distribution is linked to a high density of hormone-sensitive oil glands in these areas.

section.title: 2. Timing of Breakouts
section.description: If your acne worsens predictably around your period, ovulation, or specific hormonal events (e.g. pregnancy or stopping birth control), it’s likely hormonally influenced. In many women, breakouts begin 7–10 days before menstruation and subside once the cycle starts.

section.title: 3. Type of Lesions
section.text: Hormonal acne tends to be:
points: Cystic - deep, painful bumps that don’t come to a head
Inflammatory - red, swollen, and tender to touch
Persistent - often recurs in the same area over and over
section.paragraph: Whiteheads or blackheads may be present too, but cystic acne is a hallmark sign.

section.title: 4. Resistance to Topical Treatments
section.description: If you're using over-the-counter cleansers, benzoyl peroxide, or salicylic acid but your acne isn't improving — or seems unaffected by good skincare habits — this may point to an internal cause. Hormonal acne often doesn’t respond well to surface-level treatments alone.

section.title: 5. Acne Alongside Other Hormonal Symptoms
section.text: You may also notice:
points: Irregular or painful periods
Excess facial or body hair (hirsutism)
Hair thinning or loss
Weight gain or difficulty losing weight
Mood swings or fatigue
section.paragraph: These could indicate a broader hormonal imbalance, such as PCOS or thyroid dysfunction.

section.heading: Can Hormonal Acne Be Controlled?
section.text: Yes, but it requires a tailored approach that includes:
points: Lifestyle adjustments: stress reduction, improved sleep, blood sugar control
Diet: reducing dairy and high-sugar foods, increasing anti-inflammatory foods
Topical treatments: retinoids, niacinamide, azelaic acid
Prescription therapies: hormonal contraceptives, spironolactone, metformin (in PCOS)
Supportive skincare: non-comedogenic, barrier-supporting routines

section.heading: When To Seek Help
section.text: You should consider seeing a dermatologist or endocrinologist if:
points: Your acne has become painful, scarring, or cystic
It recurs monthly in the same areas
You experience other symptoms of hormonal imbalance
You've tried skincare products but
section.paragraph: A medical professional can order hormone testing, suggest bloodwork, or refer you for deeper investigation if needed.

description: At Clear Ritual, we take hormonal acne seriously — not just as a skin condition, but as a reflection of what’s going on inside. That’s why our approach is based on science, skincare, and systemic insight.
Take our free skin test to identify whether your acne is hormonal and get a personalized acne plan rooted in dermatology, endocrinology, and real-world results.

section.heading: Article Overview
description: Acne isn’t just something people grow out of. For many adults — particularly women — breakouts persist well into their 20s, 30s, and 40s. In fact, adult acne is increasingly common, and its causes are often more complex than those in adolescence.

This article explores what adult acne is, how it differs from teenage acne, why it tends to affect certain individuals more than others, and how it often presents — especially in the form of cystic adult acne.

section.heading: What Is Hormonal Acne?
section.description: Adult acne refers to acne that appears after the age of 25. It may be a continuation of teenage acne, or it may begin for the first time in adulthood — a pattern sometimes referred to as late-onset acne. While it affects all genders, adult acne in women is far more prevalent, particularly among those navigating hormonal changes.

section.heading: Adult Acne in Women
section.text: Women are more likely to experience acne due to the natural hormonal fluctuations associated with:
points: The menstrual cycle
Pregnancy and postpartum phases
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
Starting or stopping hormonal birth control
Perimenopause or menopause
section.paragraph: These fluctuations can stimulate excess sebum production and increase inflammation, often leading to breakouts along the chin, jawline, and cheeks — regions sensitive to hormonal shifts.

section.heading: Common Causes of Adult Acne
section.description: Understanding the causes of adult acne requires considering multiple layers — from internal physiology to external environment. Some contributing factors include:

section.title: 1. Hormonal Activity
section.description: Hormones play a central role in regulating oil production. Imbalances or sensitivities to androgens can increase sebum levels and cause persistent breakouts.

section.title: 2. Stress and the Endocrine System
section.description: Stress doesn’t directly cause acne, but it may trigger a cascade of hormonal responses — particularly increased cortisol — that influence oil production and skin inflammation.

section.title: 3. Diet and Metabolism
section.description: There is growing interest in how diet may impact acne, particularly in adults. High-glycemic foods, dairy, and certain proteins may affect insulin and androgen levels, though this varies widely between individuals.

section.title: 4. Inflammatory Conditions and Gut Health
section.description: Systemic inflammation or poor gut function may be associated with persistent adult acne, particularly in those experiencing other inflammatory symptoms like bloating or fatigue.

section.title: 5. Skincare and Product Use
section.description: Adults often use a combination of makeup, skincare, and hair products, some of which may contain comedogenic ingredients — substances that can clog pores and contribute to breakouts.

section.heading: Types of Adult Acne
section.text: While adult acne may present in many forms, certain types tend to be more common:
points: Comedonal acne: Blackheads and whiteheads caused by clogged pores
Inflammatory acne: Red, swollen pimples or papules
Cystic acne: Deep, painful nodules under the skin, often recurring in the same area
Hormonal acne: Breakouts timed with cycles, most often along the lower face
Post-inflammatory marks: Dark spots or scars that persist after acne resolves
section.paragraph: The pattern, severity, and frequency of acne in adults can differ substantially from adolescent presentations — and may be less responsive to conventional treatments.

section.heading: Why Does Adult Acne Occur Now?
section.text: For many, adult acne seems to appear without warning. In some cases, it may be triggered by life events like:
points: A change in work-life stress levels
Shifting to or off hormonal medications
A new diet or exercise routine
Moving to a new climate or environment
Sleep disruptions or altered circadian rhythm
Weight fluctuations
section.paragraph: Because acne is a symptom, not a disease, it's often the skin's way of signaling internal or external imbalance.

section.heading: Is Cystic Adult Acne Different?
description: Yes — cystic adult acne is one of the most severe forms. It presents as large, inflamed, and often painful lesions that lie deeper within the skin. These are less likely to come to a head and more likely to result in scarring or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
This type of acne tends to have a hormonal or inflammatory origin, and may not respond to over-the-counter approaches. Identifying cystic patterns early can help avoid long-term damage.

section.heading: Is There a “One Cause” of Adult Acne?
description: Rarely. Adult acne is multifactorial — meaning multiple systems in the body may be contributing at once. For some, the cause is dominantly hormonal. For others, it may be environmental, stress-related, or rooted in digestion or metabolism. Genetics, too, can influence how the skin responds to internal changes.

section.heading: Exploring Adult Acne Without Quick Fixes
description: Understanding how to treat adult acne isn’t just about applying stronger creams or switching cleansers. Because its causes are varied and layered, treatment often starts with investigation, not assumption. That means observing patterns, tracking symptoms, and — in many cases — consulting with a professional.

section.heading: A Note from the Clear Ritual Team
section.text: At Clear Ritual, we believe acne is not something to be fought — it’s something to be understood. If you're facing recurring or resistant adult acne, the first step is not to treat blindly, but to explore:
points: What patterns do you notice?
What changes in your health or lifestyle have occurred recently?
How does your acne respond across your cycle, stress levels, or habits?
section.paragraph: We’ve designed a skin test that helps map out these patterns. No diagnosis. No overpromising. Just a structured starting point for you — and your skin — to work with clarity.

section.heading: Article Overview
description: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is a hormonal condition that affects nearly 1 in 5 women of reproductive age — and one of its most visible signs is persistent acne. Unlike typical breakouts, PCOS acne often follows a specific pattern, shows resistance to conventional treatments, and may be a sign of deeper hormonal imbalances.
In this article, we explore what PCOS acne looks like, why it occurs, and what emerging insights say about diet, lifestyle, and long-term management.

section.heading: Why Does PCOS Cause Acne?
section.text: PCOS is characterized by elevated levels of androgens (male hormones such as testosterone), which can:
points: Stimulate sebaceous (oil) glands
Increase oil production
Disrupt normal skin cell turnover
Create an environment for clogged pores and inflammation
section.paragraph: This hormonal activity leads to chronic, inflammatory acne, typically affecting the ,strong>lower half of the face.

section.heading: What Does PCOS Acne Look Like?
section.text: While it can vary, PCOS acne typically presents as:
points: Deep, cystic pimples
Painful nodules under the skin
Persistent breakouts that don't easily come to a head
Located along the <strong>jawline, chin, and sometimes neck,/strong>
section.paragraph: This distinct distribution is often referred to as PCOS jawline acne and is a hallmark of androgen-driven breakouts.

section.heading: What Is the PCOS Acne Pattern?
section.text: Many individuals report a consistent PCOS acne pattern, which may include:
points: Monthly flare-ups, often in the
Long-lasting pimples that recur in the same areas
Post-inflammatory marks that take time to fade
Resistance to over-the-counter treatments like salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide
section.paragraph: Unlike teenage acne, which often focuses on the forehead and nose, PCOS-related acne tends to concentrate on the lower face.

section.heading: How to Approach PCOS Acne
section.text: You may come across personal stories like "how I cured my PCOS acne" — and while these experiences are valid, it's important to understand that PCOS is a complex, long-term condition. Acne related to PCOS may improve or worsen depending on:
points: Hormonal regulation
Lifestyle changes
Gut and metabolic health
Weight shifts and insulin sensitivity
Medication or natural therapies under medical supervision
section.paragraph: For some, acne improves significantly with targeted approaches. For others, it becomes a long-term condition to manage.

section.heading: Does PCOS Acne Ever Go Away?
description: The answer is: it depends. In some individuals, PCOS acne may resolve over time, especially if hormone levels stabilize through lifestyle or medical support. In others, it may persist or fluctuate across life stages, including pregnancy, postpartum, or perimenopause.

Since PCOS itself doesn't have a permanent "cure," its skin-related symptoms often reflect what's happening hormonally, metabolically, and systemically. Acne is simply one expression of this imbalance.

section.heading: How to Control PCOS Acne
section.text: Controlling PCOS-related acne often begins with understanding your body's patterns:
points: Are breakouts linked to stress, diet, or cycle?
Do they appear at the same time each month?
Have recent weight changes impacted your skin?
Are there other symptoms — like hair thinning, irregular periods, or bloating — accompanying the acne?
section.paragraph: These questions help contextualize acne as part of a broader hormonal picture, rather than just a surface-level issue.

section.heading: The Role of Diet in PCOS Acne
section.text: There is growing research interest in the connection between diet and PCOS acne. While findings vary, some themes include:
points: Low-glycemic diets may help stabilize insulin and androgen levels
Dairy reduction (especially skim milk) has been anecdotally linked to clearer skin in some
Anti-inflammatory diets rich in fiber, omega-3s, and micronutrients may support hormonal balance
Excess sugar and processed foods may contribute to flare-ups in sensitive individuals
section.paragraph: Still, diet's effect on acne is highly individual. What works for one person may not work for another — and restrictive approaches can sometimes backfire. Working with a qualified practitioner is essential if considering dietary changes.

section.heading: How to Treat PCOS Acne Naturally
section.text: Many individuals seek natural ways to manage PCOS acne, focusing on long-term, sustainable changes. These may include:
points: Supporting hormone balance through sleep, stress management, and cycle tracking
Identifying gut or metabolic triggers through elimination or functional testing
Evaluating skincare products for comedogenic ingredients
Exploring supplements, herbs, or adaptogens under professional guidance
Incorporating non-inflammatory routines that don't disrupt the skin barrier
section.paragraph: Again, while natural strategies can be powerful, PCOS is a hormonal condition that benefits from personalized and informed guidance.
